title: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State
sourceTitle: The management of the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) in adults with diabetes
locator: PDF pages 12 to 32 and care pathway pages 38 to 42: diagnostic criteria, fluid replacement, insulin, potassium replacement, monitoring and resolution
scope: Adults with HHS in hospital; this limited extraction covers diagnostic features, severity assessment, early fluid and electrolyte management, fixed-rate intravenous insulin when indicated, monitoring and resolution.
gaps: The guideline requires clinical judgement for frail adults, people aged 18 to 25 years, pregnancy, heart failure, renal failure and mixed DKA/HHS. The encoded insulin regimen is limited to adult HHS after adequate fluid replacement; complete medicine contraindications, local pump preparation policy and thromboprophylaxis dose are not established by this extraction. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Does the biochemical and clinical picture support HHS rather than DKA or another cause of hyperglycaemia?
investigations.finding: Typical HHS features are marked hypovolaemia, glucose 30 mmol/L or more, osmolality usually 320 mOsm/kg or more, ketones 3 mmol/L or less, pH 7.3 or more and bicarbonate 15 mmol/L or more.
investigations.rationale: HHS and mixed DKA/HHS require different insulin timing and rates.
investigations.timeframe: At presentation before treatment, without delaying urgent resuscitation

investigations.question: Are there features requiring high-dependency or level 2 care?
investigations.finding: Escalation features include osmolality above 350 mOsm/kg, sodium above 160 mmol/L, pH below 7.1, potassium below 3.5 or above 6 mmol/L, GCS below 12, oxygen saturation below 92%, systolic pressure below 90 mmHg, pulse above 100 or below 60, urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour, creatinine above 200 micromol/L or acute kidney injury.
investigations.rationale: Severe biochemical or physiological disturbance predicts complications and need for closer monitoring.
investigations.timeframe: At admission and repeatedly during early treatment

investigations.test: Serial glucose, calculated osmolality and electrolytes
investigations.question: Are fluid and insulin therapy correcting hyperosmolality at a safe rate?
investigations.finding: Target an osmolality fall of 3 to 8 mOsm/kg/hour and a glucose fall no faster than 5 mmol/L/hour; assess sodium, potassium, renal function, fluid balance, cognition and urine output.
investigations.rationale: Rapid osmotic change and potassium disturbance can cause neurological or cardiac harm.
investigations.timeframe: Hourly in the initial phase, then at intervals directed by response and local protocol

actions.instruction: Give 0.9% sodium chloride 1 litre intravenously over the first hour, using slower replacement when appropriate in younger adults, older or frail people, pregnancy, heart failure or renal failure; then individualise replacement against osmolality, sodium, haemodynamics and fluid balance.
actions.timeframe: Immediately after assessment

actions.instruction: Do not start insulin immediately in pure HHS without significant ketonaemia; restore circulating volume first. If glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, add 5% or 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour while continuing 0.9% sodium chloride as required.
actions.timeframe: During initial fluid treatment and subsequent glucose fall

actions.instruction: Use holistic resolution criteria: osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg, hypovolaemia corrected with urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour, cognition returned to baseline and glucose below 15 mmol/L; complete resolution may take up to 72 hours.
actions.timeframe: Before transition from acute HHS treatment

medicines.indication: Fixed-rate insulin infusion for adult HHS after adequate fluid replacement when insulin is indicated
medicines.group: Adults with HHS who have stopped responding to initial fluid replacement or have significant ketonaemia, excluding mixed DKA/HHS managed under the DKA pathway
medicines.dose: 0.05 units/kg/hour, prepared as 50 units made up to 50 mL with 0.9% sodium chloride
medicines.duration: After adequate fluid replacement until holistic HHS resolution and safe transition from intravenous treatment
adjustments: For mixed DKA/HHS, follow the DKA pathway using 0.1 units/kg/hour.
Delay insulin in pure HHS until adequate fluid replacement and reassessment because early insulin can cause circulatory collapse and rapid osmotic change.
When glucose is below 14 mmol/L, add 5% or 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour and continue 0.9% sodium chloride according to fluid status.
monitoring: Monitor glucose, calculated osmolality, sodium and potassium frequently, hourly during the initial phase.
Target glucose fall no faster than 5 mmol/L/hour and osmolality fall 3 to 8 mOsm/kg/hour.
Monitor fluid balance, cognition, haemodynamics and urine output.

title: Hypertension in Adults [Adapted from NICE]
sourceTitle: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management
scope: Adults undergoing diagnosis, cardiovascular-risk assessment and management of primary hypertension; pregnancy and specialist secondary-hypertension pathways are outside this limited extraction.
gaps: NICE thresholds and risk tools require reconciliation with current Saudi policy and local formulary. Drug classes are named but complete dose, route, frequency, duration, interaction and contraindication sets are not supplied, so no medication regimen is encoded. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.test: Clinic blood pressure followed by ABPM or HBPM
investigations.question: Is persistent hypertension confirmed outside the clinic?
investigations.finding: For clinic blood pressure from 140/90 to 180/120 mmHg, offer ambulatory monitoring; use home monitoring if ambulatory monitoring is unsuitable. Confirm when clinic pressure is at least 140/90 and daytime ambulatory or home average is at least 135/85 mmHg.
investigations.rationale: Out-of-office measurement reduces misclassification from clinic-only readings.
investigations.timeframe: During diagnostic confirmation

investigations.question: Has hypertension caused renal, retinal or cardiac injury and what is the person's cardiovascular risk?
investigations.finding: Assess urine albumin:creatinine ratio and haematuria, HbA1c, electrolytes, creatinine/eGFR, cholesterol, fundi and 12-lead ECG, and estimate cardiovascular risk.
investigations.rationale: Organ damage and risk influence treatment urgency and targets.
investigations.timeframe: At confirmed diagnosis and as clinically indicated

investigations.question: Does blood pressure at or above 180/120 mmHg have retinal, neurological, cardiac or renal emergency features?
investigations.finding: Same-day specialist assessment is required when severe hypertension is accompanied by retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, confusion, chest pain, heart failure or acute kidney injury.
investigations.rationale: Acute target-organ injury requires urgent specialist treatment.
investigations.timeframe: Immediately when severe hypertension is identified

actions.instruction: Set clinic targets below 140/90 mmHg for adults under 80 and below 150/90 mmHg for adults aged 80 or older, with lower corresponding home or ambulatory targets and individualisation for frailty or multimorbidity.
actions.timeframe: During treatment and review

actions.instruction: Do not use an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker in pregnancy; use current pregnancy-specific and local prescribing guidance.
actions.timeframe: Before prescribing and when pregnancy is possible

title: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
sourceTitle: Hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management
locator: Recommendations 1.1.2, 1.2.1 to 1.2.14, 1.3.1 to 1.3.19, Tables 1 and 2, and 1.5.1 to 1.5.25
scope: Pregnant women with chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension or suspected pre-eclampsia; this limited extraction covers risk reduction, assessment, surveillance and escalation.
gaps: Aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks and labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa are recommended in defined circumstances, but the source does not supply a complete route, exact regimen for all indications, interaction and contraindication set, so no medication regimen is encoded. Local obstetric emergency thresholds, formulary and fetal-surveillance protocols must be reconciled. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.test: Maternal blood pressure, urinalysis and laboratory assessment
investigations.question: Is gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia present and is maternal organ dysfunction developing?
investigations.finding: Assess blood pressure and proteinuria, and obtain full blood count, liver function and renal function according to the disorder and severity.
investigations.rationale: Maternal hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia and renal or hepatic dysfunction determine diagnosis, surveillance and escalation.
investigations.timeframe: At presentation and repeated according to severity and specialist plan

investigations.question: Can suspected pre-eclampsia between 20 weeks and 36 weeks plus 6 days be clarified?
investigations.finding: Offer a single placental growth factor-based test to help rule out pre-eclampsia when it is suspected in this gestational window.
investigations.rationale: Placental biomarker testing can support diagnostic triage alongside clinical assessment.
investigations.timeframe: Once per episode of suspected pre-eclampsia in the specified gestational window

investigations.test: Ultrasound fetal growth and wellbeing assessment
investigations.question: Is hypertension affecting fetal growth, amniotic fluid or placental circulation?
investigations.finding: Use fetal biometry, amniotic-fluid assessment and umbilical-artery Doppler according to the hypertensive disorder and gestation.
investigations.rationale: Placental dysfunction can cause fetal growth restriction and influence timing of birth.
investigations.timeframe: At diagnosis and repeated according to the NICE tables and clinical findings

actions.instruction: For chronic hypertension in pregnancy, aim for a blood pressure target of 135/85 mmHg and arrange specialist antenatal review and surveillance.
actions.timeframe: Throughout pregnancy once treatment is required

actions.instruction: Stop ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers within 2 working days of pregnancy notification and offer an alternative suitable for pregnancy.
actions.timeframe: As soon as pregnancy is known

actions.instruction: Escalate severe hypertension, maternal organ dysfunction, concerning symptoms or fetal compromise urgently to obstetric specialist care and plan timing of birth through senior multidisciplinary assessment.
actions.timeframe: Immediately when severe or deteriorating features occur

title: Hypothyroidism
scope: Adults with suspected or confirmed primary hypothyroidism; this limited extraction covers biochemical testing, thyroid peroxidase antibodies, levothyroxine initiation principles and monitoring.
gaps: NICE gives levothyroxine starting doses of 1.6 micrograms/kg/day for adults under 65 without cardiovascular disease and 25 to 50 micrograms/day for adults aged 65 or older or with cardiovascular disease, but does not state a complete route, interaction and contraindication set in these recommendations, so no medication regimen is encoded. Pregnancy, severe illness, pituitary disease and paediatric care require separate pathways. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Does thyroid biochemistry support primary hypothyroidism?
investigations.finding: Measure TSH alone in adults when pituitary disease is not suspected, then measure free T4 in the same sample if TSH is above range; measure both TSH and free T4 when secondary thyroid dysfunction is suspected.
investigations.rationale: Test selection distinguishes primary from possible central thyroid dysfunction.
investigations.timeframe: At initial assessment; do not repeat within 6 weeks unless clinically necessary

investigations.question: Is autoimmune thyroid disease a likely cause of raised TSH?
investigations.finding: Consider measuring thyroid peroxidase antibodies when TSH is above the reference range, but do not routinely repeat the test.
investigations.rationale: Autoantibody status can support aetiology and decisions in subclinical disease.
investigations.timeframe: Once after raised TSH when clinically relevant

investigations.question: Has levothyroxine normalised TSH without causing biochemical over-treatment?
investigations.finding: Measure TSH every 3 months until stable, then once a year; consider free T4 as well if symptoms persist.
investigations.rationale: Dose requirements change over time and both under-treatment and TSH suppression can cause harm.
investigations.timeframe: Every 3 months until stable, then annually

actions.instruction: Offer levothyroxine as first-line treatment for primary hypothyroidism and adjust to maintain TSH within the reference range while avoiding TSH suppression or thyrotoxicosis.
actions.timeframe: After biochemical confirmation and during follow-up

actions.instruction: Ask about biotin supplement use because high intake can cause misleading thyroid test results; use specialist pathways when pituitary disease, pregnancy or severe illness is suspected.
actions.timeframe: Before interpreting thyroid tests

title: Intrapartum Fetal Compromise
locator: Recommendations 1.3.1 to 1.3.12, 1.4.3 to 1.4.38, Tables 1 to 3 and 1.5.1 to 1.5.11
scope: Women in labour requiring fetal monitoring; this limited extraction covers risk assessment, CTG interpretation, escalation and urgent response to acute bradycardia or prolonged deceleration.
gaps: CTG interpretation must be integrated with the whole clinical picture, gestation and local obstetric escalation policy. The source names measures such as stopping oxytocin but does not provide a complete medication regimen or contraindication set, so no medicine regimen is encoded. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Have maternal, fetal or labour risk factors emerged that require continuous CTG or escalation?
investigations.finding: Perform and document a systematic assessment at least hourly and use a second clinician for a fresh-eyes review of continuous CTG at least hourly.
investigations.rationale: Risk and fetal response can change rapidly during labour.
investigations.timeframe: At least hourly during labour

investigations.question: How should contractions, baseline rate, variability and decelerations be classified?
investigations.finding: Classify each CTG feature using the white, amber and red criteria and combine the features with the clinical context to describe the trace as normal, suspicious or pathological.
investigations.rationale: A common structured vocabulary supports consistent escalation and response.
investigations.timeframe: Continuously, with formal documented review at least hourly

investigations.test: Acute bradycardia or prolonged deceleration assessment
investigations.question: Has fetal heart rate fallen acutely for 3 minutes or longer?
investigations.finding: An acute bradycardia or a single prolonged deceleration lasting 3 minutes or more requires urgent obstetric review and preparation for urgent birth.
investigations.rationale: Persistent acute heart-rate reduction may indicate rapidly developing fetal hypoxia.
investigations.timeframe: Immediate recognition and response

actions.instruction: For a suspicious or pathological CTG, undertake urgent review of reversible causes and the whole clinical picture, escalate according to severity and document the plan and review interval.
actions.timeframe: Immediately after abnormal classification

actions.instruction: For acute bradycardia or prolonged deceleration lasting 3 minutes or more, call for urgent obstetric help, prepare for urgent birth and expedite birth if recovery is inadequate or other risk factors persist.
actions.timeframe: Immediately

actions.instruction: When CTG concerns arise in active second stage, consider stopping oxytocin and discourage pushing unless birth is imminent while urgent senior review proceeds.
actions.timeframe: During active second stage when concerns occur

title: Ischaemic Heart Disease
scope: Adults with stable angina due to atherosclerotic coronary disease; this limited extraction covers symptom review, secondary prevention, antianginal treatment principles and revascularisation assessment.
gaps: This older UK guideline must be reconciled with current ESC, ACC/AHA and Saudi guidance, contemporary chronic-coronary-syndrome diagnostics, lipid targets, antiplatelet practice and revascularisation evidence. Aspirin 75 mg daily and short-acting nitrates are mentioned, but the source does not provide complete route, duration, interaction and contraindication sets, so no medication regimen is encoded. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Are symptoms consistent with stable angina and are frequency, triggers and functional impact changing?
investigations.finding: Review the diagnosis, symptom burden, adherence, adverse effects and modifiable risk factors when starting or adjusting treatment.
investigations.rationale: Worsening or atypical symptoms can require a different acute or diagnostic pathway.
investigations.timeframe: At presentation and 2 to 4 weeks after starting or changing treatment

investigations.test: Coronary anatomy and functional assessment when symptoms persist
investigations.question: Would angiography and functional testing alter revascularisation decisions?
investigations.finding: When symptoms are not satisfactorily controlled with optimal medical treatment, offer coronary angiography to guide treatment and use additional functional testing if required.
investigations.rationale: Anatomy, ischaemia and clinical factors determine whether CABG, PCI or continued medical therapy is appropriate.
investigations.timeframe: After inadequate symptom control or when prognostic anatomy is suspected

investigations.question: Do anatomy, diabetes, age, comorbidity and procedural suitability favour CABG, PCI or continued medical care?
investigations.finding: Complex left-main or three-vessel disease and uncertain strategy should be reviewed by cardiac surgeons and interventional cardiologists.
investigations.rationale: Balanced specialist review supports informed selection of the revascularisation strategy.
investigations.timeframe: Before elective revascularisation

actions.instruction: Provide a short-acting nitrate for angina episodes and explain that the dose may be repeated after 5 minutes; call an emergency ambulance if pain persists 5 minutes after the second dose.
actions.timeframe: At diagnosis and reinforced at review

actions.instruction: Offer a beta blocker or calcium-channel blocker as first-line regular antianginal treatment, selected according to comorbidity, contraindications and preference, and review response 2 to 4 weeks after starting or changing therapy.
actions.timeframe: During symptom management

actions.instruction: Discuss revascularisation when symptoms remain uncontrolled despite optimal treatment, using shared decisions on symptom relief, procedure risks, repeat intervention and possible prognostic benefit.
actions.timeframe: After inadequate control with medical treatment

title: Kidney Failure Planning and Dialysis Access
sourceTitle: Renal replacement therapy and conservative management
scope: Adults approaching kidney failure who are choosing between conservative care and renal replacement therapy; this limited extraction covers shared decisions, timing of dialysis and access planning.
gaps: This 2018 UK guideline requires reconciliation with current Saudi nephrology policy, transplant pathways, vascular mapping standards, access-service capacity and updated evidence. It does not verify anticoagulation, antimicrobial, anaemia, mineral-bone or dialysis prescription regimens. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: When is kidney replacement therapy likely to be needed and are symptoms or biochemical abnormalities becoming refractory?
investigations.finding: Assess symptoms, biochemical measures, fluid status and eGFR together; dialysis may be needed for symptoms, uncontrolled biochemistry or fluid overload, or at eGFR around 5 to 7 mL/min/1.73 m² if no symptoms are present.
investigations.rationale: Dialysis initiation should reflect clinical need rather than an isolated eGFR value.
investigations.timeframe: Repeated during advanced chronic kidney disease and before planned initiation

investigations.question: Which option best fits prognosis, comorbidity, lifestyle, preferences and support?
investigations.finding: Discuss haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, transplantation and conservative management using individual clinical and personal factors.
investigations.rationale: The preferred treatment depends on benefits, burdens, feasibility and the person's goals.
investigations.timeframe: Start assessment at least 1 year before renal replacement therapy is likely

investigations.question: Which access type and site can be created in time for the chosen modality?
investigations.finding: Use vascular assessment including ultrasound when needed to plan an arteriovenous fistula, and assess the abdomen and practical suitability for peritoneal access.
investigations.rationale: Early planning reduces unplanned catheter-dependent dialysis and failed access.
investigations.timeframe: Plan arteriovenous fistula creation about 6 months before expected dialysis; insert an open surgical peritoneal catheter about 2 weeks before anticipated use

actions.instruction: Begin assessment for renal replacement therapy or conservative management at least 1 year before therapy is likely to be needed, including transplant assessment when appropriate.
actions.timeframe: During advanced chronic kidney disease

actions.instruction: Base dialysis initiation on symptoms, biochemical measures, uncontrollable fluid overload and estimated GFR together, through a joint decision with the person and clinical team.
actions.timeframe: When kidney failure is approaching or complications become refractory

title: Last Days of Life Care
sourceTitle: Care of dying adults in the last days of life
scope: Adults thought to be entering the last days of life; this limited extraction covers recognition of dying, individualised care planning, hydration, medicine review and symptom reassessment.
gaps: This UK guideline requires reconciliation with current Saudi law, local goals-of-care processes, family communication, spiritual care, specialist palliative services and medication protocols. It recommends symptom treatment but does not provide complete medicine dose, route, frequency, duration and contraindication sets, so no regimen is encoded. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Is the person likely to be entering the last days of life, recovering, or clinically uncertain?
investigations.finding: Assess changes in function, consciousness, breathing, intake, circulation and other clinical signs, seek reversible causes and communicate uncertainty when prognosis is unclear.
investigations.rationale: Care should respond to the person's condition without making an unsupported prognostic assumption.
investigations.timeframe: At suspected entry into the last days and whenever the condition changes

investigations.question: Which physical, psychological, social, spiritual and communication needs matter now?
investigations.finding: Create and update an individualised care plan covering goals, preferences, symptom control, hydration, current medicines and preferred place of care.
investigations.rationale: Priorities and treatment burdens differ between people and can change rapidly.
investigations.timeframe: At least daily and after any material clinical change

investigations.test: Hydration and clinically assisted hydration review
investigations.question: Is dehydration causing distress, can oral intake help, and is assisted hydration benefiting or harming the person?
investigations.finding: Assess hydration daily, support drinking if desired and safe, and consider a therapeutic trial of clinically assisted hydration when distressing symptoms may relate to dehydration and oral intake is inadequate.
investigations.rationale: Hydration may relieve symptoms but can also cause fluid overload or other harm.
investigations.timeframe: Review at least daily; monitor an assisted-hydration trial at least every 12 hours

actions.instruction: Review all current medicines and stop those that are not providing symptomatic benefit or may cause harm; avoid investigations unlikely to affect care in the last days of life.
actions.timeframe: At recognition and daily review

actions.instruction: Use the least invasive suitable route for symptom medicines, avoid intramuscular injections, and consider subcutaneous or intravenous delivery when oral medicines are unsuitable; consider a syringe pump if more than 2 or 3 as-needed doses are required in 24 hours.
actions.timeframe: During symptom management

actions.instruction: Use the lowest effective symptom-relief dose, reassess at least daily, seek specialist palliative advice when symptoms do not improve promptly, and reduce or stop clinically assisted hydration if harm occurs.
actions.timeframe: Daily and after each treatment change

title: Lung Cancer Management
locator: Diagnosis and staging recommendations 1.2.1 to 1.2.27, including CT, tissue sampling, PET-CT and mediastinal staging
scope: Adults with suspected or confirmed lung cancer; this limited extraction covers diagnostic imaging, tissue acquisition, molecular-pathology adequacy and staging before treatment selection.
gaps: The NICE staging recommendations cite AJCC TNM seventh edition and therefore require reconciliation with the current TNM edition, Saudi oncology standards and local multidisciplinary pathways. This extraction does not verify surgery, radiotherapy or systemic anticancer drug regimens. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.test: Contrast-enhanced CT of chest and upper abdomen
investigations.question: What is the likely primary tumour extent and are nodal, liver or adrenal metastases visible?
investigations.finding: Perform contrast-enhanced CT including the liver, adrenal glands and lower neck before biopsy when possible, with caution in renal impairment.
investigations.rationale: Early staging information guides the safest biopsy target and avoids tests that will not alter treatment.
investigations.timeframe: Before tissue sampling when clinically feasible

investigations.test: Tissue diagnosis with subtype and molecular-marker adequacy
investigations.question: Can the selected procedure provide enough material for diagnosis, histological subtype and relevant molecular testing?
investigations.finding: Choose investigations that give the most information about diagnosis and stage with the least risk, and obtain samples adequate for pathological subtyping and molecular-marker testing.
investigations.rationale: Treatment selection depends on accurate histology, stage and actionable biomarkers.
investigations.timeframe: During initial diagnostic work-up

investigations.test: PET-CT and invasive mediastinal staging when indicated
investigations.question: Is curative-intent treatment plausible and do mediastinal nodes require pathological confirmation?
investigations.finding: Offer PET-CT before curative-intent treatment and use EBUS-TBNA, EUS-FNA or surgical staging according to nodal size, PET uptake and whether results would change treatment.
investigations.rationale: Accurate nodal and distant staging prevents futile treatment and supports definitive planning.
investigations.timeframe: Before definitive curative-intent treatment

actions.instruction: Plan the diagnostic sequence to maximise combined diagnosis and staging information while minimising risk and delay, and avoid a biopsy target that provides less staging information when a more informative target is available.
actions.timeframe: At multidisciplinary diagnostic planning

actions.instruction: Review confirmed lung cancer in a specialist multidisciplinary team with imaging, pathology, performance status, comorbidity, pulmonary reserve and patient preferences available before treatment selection.
actions.timeframe: Before definitive treatment

title: Malignant Bowel Obstruction Support
sourceTitle: MASCC multidisciplinary evidence-based recommendations for the management of malignant bowel obstruction in advanced cancer
locator: Table 3 and sections on antiemetics, corticosteroids, decompression, nutrition, hydration and surgery
scope: Adults with malignant bowel obstruction in advanced cancer; this limited extraction covers assessment, symptom support, decompression, nutrition and selection for procedural or surgical intervention.
gaps: The guideline names octreotide, lanreotide, metoclopramide and dexamethasone and gives a dexamethasone dose range of 4 to 16 mg daily with discontinuation after 3 to 5 days if ineffective, but does not supply a complete route, frequency, interaction and contraindication set for an exact regimen. No medicine regimen is encoded. Decisions require current local oncology, surgical, palliative and pharmacy review. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.test: Clinical and imaging confirmation of obstruction
investigations.question: Is obstruction partial or complete, single-level or multi-level, and is a reversible or emergent surgical cause present?
investigations.finding: Assess symptoms, hydration, performance status, prognosis, cancer extent and imaging-defined obstruction before selecting supportive, endoscopic or surgical management.
investigations.rationale: Completeness, level, disease burden and goals determine whether prokinetic treatment, decompression, stenting or surgery is appropriate.
investigations.timeframe: At presentation and with clinical deterioration

investigations.question: What are the burdens of nausea, vomiting, pain, distension, dehydration and inability to eat or drink?
investigations.finding: Assess symptoms and nutritional status individually and align hydration or nutrition interventions with prognosis, expected benefit, burdens and goals of care.
investigations.rationale: Routine artificial hydration or nutrition may not improve outcomes and can cause complications, especially near end of life.
investigations.timeframe: At admission and repeatedly during supportive care

investigations.test: Suitability for decompression, stent or surgery
investigations.question: Would nasogastric decompression, venting gastrostomy, self-expanding metal stent or surgery provide net benefit?
investigations.finding: Use temporary nasogastric decompression for acute obstruction, consider venting gastrostomy for longer-term decompression, prefer a stent for suitable single-level large-bowel obstruction, and reserve surgery for highly selected patients.
investigations.rationale: Interventions differ in invasiveness, durability, complication risk and likely benefit.
investigations.timeframe: Early multidisciplinary review after initial stabilisation

actions.instruction: Keep the person nil by mouth initially, provide symptom-led decompression and supportive care, then reintroduce oral intake gradually when obstruction improves and symptoms permit.
actions.timeframe: During the acute episode and recovery

actions.instruction: Avoid metoclopramide in complete malignant bowel obstruction because of possible perforation risk; somatostatin analogues may reduce vomiting, and corticosteroids may offer short-term symptom benefit only after local medicine review.
actions.timeframe: During medication selection

actions.instruction: Use parenteral hydration or nutrition only in selected people when expected benefit outweighs burden; do not initiate these routinely at the end of life.
actions.timeframe: At goals-of-care and nutrition review
